opening.headline: In AI services, service objectives (SLO) that determine what is a problem, incident definition, recording, on-call system, and incident response guidelines are connected into one response flow.
body: Imagine that ten response error rate warnings go off at once in the early morning. There is no documentation about who is in charge or who to contact, and people are looking at different dashboards and giving different reasons. The damage increases without knowing what to do first.

In this class, we will first look at how to establish standards for service failures using SLI and SLO. Next, the NIST Glossary defines an incident, audit trail, and incident response guidance (NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3) confirms the view of response as part of risk management. Next, we summarize the on-call system through which notifications reach people and the timeline of failure response, and explain cases of prioritization by scope of impact, reasons for different responses over cost and quality, and cases of post-mortem analysis using records.
The reference materials are centered on the NIST glossary and guidance documents, so explanations focus on the general concept of response rather than product-specific functions.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the role SLOs, incident definitions, and audit trails play in response
Scope of influence and service goals can explain why response order and call targets are determined
Error budget and burn rate quantify the SLO threat level and explain why delay SLI is defined as a percentile.

screens.title: I have a disability and don't know who to call first.
screens.lead: Open each item to see the chaos that occurs when early morning warnings pour in.

visual.alt: A picture of ten alerts going off at once, candidates in charge with question marks, and different dashboards scattered around.

items.title: Warnings sound all at once
items.body: At dawn, ten response error rate warnings sound simultaneously. More warnings don't mean 10 problems. A single cause may be reflected in multiple indicators, or it may be a mixture of unrelated factors. If you don't have a baseline to determine what's important, you'll open the alerts that stand out first.

items.title: There is no contact route with the person in charge
items.body: There is no documentation on who is responsible for this service or who to contact again if I don't receive it. While you spend time looking for people, obstacles take over. The first condition for response is to determine in advance the route by which notifications will reach people.

items.title: Everyone looks in a different place
items.body: Everyone opens their own dashboard and talks about different causes. Unless we look at the same incident through the same record, we cannot reach a consensus. Having a common record that allows us to reconstruct events chronologically allows us to discuss facts rather than speculation.

items.title: What this class covers
items.body: It covers in order the standards for defining failures (SLO), classification and definition of incidents, chronological records (audit trails), the system by which notifications reach people (on-call), and the flow of response. What they all have in common is that they are prepared before a disability occurs.

screens.outro: Most of the confusion at dawn comes from standards, communication routes, and common records that were not established before the incident occurred. The following screens cover how to prepare these three one by one.

screens.title: Think back: The first 10 minutes of that night.
screens.lead: Look at each question, think of your own answer first, and then select an item to see what you can think about. You will not enter or submit an answer.

items.prompt: Have you ever been in a similar situation where you had a disability and didn't know who to call or what to look at first?
items.answer: In such situations, system is often lacking rather than technology. The first few minutes could have been saved if we had established who was coordinating the response and what metrics were being looked at.

items.prompt: What was the first thing you did in those first 10 minutes, and what was that choice based on?
items.answer: If the basis is not the goal or scope of influence, but rather which notification arrived first, then priority is left to chance. The following screens show you how to determine ordering based on impact and service goals.

items.prompt: Were there any records left to later reconstruct what happened and in what order?
items.answer: Without records to reconstruct, post-mortem analysis relies on memory, and prevention of recurrence is built on guesswork. This is why records remaining in chronological order from the time of the incident are necessary.

screens.outro: What comes to mind is not saved anywhere, so you can honestly look back on your past experiences. What was disappointing soon becomes a list of items to prepare.

screens.title: SLO: Determine importance based on service goals
screens.lead: Select each tab to see how metrics (SLI) become objectives (SLO) and those objectives determine the urgency of the response.

tabs.label: SLI
tabs.body: SLI is a measure of service behavior from the user's perspective. It translates what the user feels, such as response delay and request success rate, into numbers. Values ​​that measure internal states, such as a server's CPU utilization, are useful when finding the cause, but they do not directly tell you what the user is experiencing.

tabs.label: SLO
tabs.body: SLO is a promise made as a goal of reliability by linking SLI to business values. For example, write that a certain percentage of requests will be responded to within a certain amount of time. Only by having a goal can you determine whether what is happening now is a disorder or a fluctuation within the normal range.

tabs.label: SLI in AI services
tabs.body: In AI services, not only response delay and success rate but also response quality can be SLI. Even if the server responds normally, if the answer is wrong, the user feels that the service is not working properly. Therefore, setting service goals based on uptime alone will ensure that quality issues are not an obstacle.

tabs.label: urgency
tabs.body: The level of threat to the SLO determines the urgency of the response. Mild wobbles that leave room for the goal are dealt with during work hours, and conditions that threaten to soon violate the goal are called in immediately. SLO is the standard for not reacting to all warnings with the same intensity. Error budget and burn rate are ways to quantify the threat level.

screens.outro: Let's now look at how to quantify the threat level and how to define delayed SLI.

screens.title: Error Budgets and Burn Rates: How to Turn SLO into Response Urgency
screens.lead: Move the slider to see how quickly failures pile up at 99.9% SLO, reducing your error budget and how that affects whether you call someone or ticket someone. Numbers are examples assuming a 30-day period.

stops.body: If your SLO is 99.9%, you will still meet your goal even if 0.1% of requests fail. This amount of allowed failures is the error budget. The total downtime for a 30-day period is approximately 43 minutes. The error budget does not require 100% cleanliness, but rather determines how much of the allowed failures have been used and how much is left. If you have budget left, you can afford to deploy changes, and if you have little, you prioritize stabilization.

Burn rate is the rate at which the budget is consumed expressed as a multiple of the rate allowed by the SLO. A burn rate of 1 maintains a failure rate of exactly 0.1%, and the budget runs out at the end of the period, so the goal is just around the corner. It's not urgent, but if you do it consistently, you'll eventually use up your budget.

If the failure rate remains at 0.2%, the burn rate is 2, and the budget runs out in 15 days. You'll miss your goal before half the period is up, so you'll need to find the cause within a few days, but not so urgently that it'll wake you up in the middle of the night.

If the failure rate remains at 1%, the burn rate is 10 and the budget is exhausted in 3 days. Even with the same SLO, the faster it is consumed, the higher the urgency. At this level, you need to call someone and respond immediately.

A burn rate of 14.4 burns about 2% of your monthly budget in one hour. It is used as an example of a first baseline immediate call with a 99.9% SLO and a 30 day period. At this time, if you send a notification only when both the long window (1 hour) and the short window (5 minutes) exceed the criteria, you can reduce the number of continuous notifications about incidents that have already ended.

If a task takes about one day to complete and persists for three consecutive days, it consumes approximately 10% of the budget. While it doesn't require waking up personnel, neglecting it would reduce the budget, so such tasks are left as tickets during business hours. In summary, if consumption is rapid, call immediately; if slow, divide it into tickets. This distinction forms the basis for determining urgency in on-call routing.

The same concept applies to response quality. As a hypothetical example, if the SLI's target is 99% pass rate, 1% of responses may fall short, and that 1% is the quality error budget. If the pass rate drops sharply after changing the prompt and the budget decreases rapidly, it is treated as urgently as with delayed SLI, and if it decreases slowly, it is left as an improvement item.

screens.outro: The error budget addressed the volume of failure. Now we'll look at how to define delayed SLIs to reflect the actual customer experience.

ext.title: Google SRE Workbook: Alerting on SLOs
Google SRE Book: Service Level Objectives

screens.title: Latency SLI is defined as a percentile, not an average
screens.lead: Toggle the setting to compare what differs when viewing the same 100 requests on average versus at the percentile level. The numbers are assumptions for illustrative purposes.

states.label: On average
states.body: Assumption: Out of 100 requests, 94 took 2 seconds and 6 took 40 seconds. The average delay is approximately 4.3 seconds. This value represents a number that no user actually experienced. Most users experienced 2 seconds, while a few experienced 40 seconds; the average combines these two values into a number that no individual user actually encountered. Even if slow requests increase from 6 to 12, the average remains only slightly higher at about 6.6 seconds, and may not trigger an alert threshold. Similarly, the overall quality average masks performance drops among certain customer segments. For instance, even if the pass rate of the 5% of customers drops from 90% to 40%, the overall pass rate only decreases from approximately 97.6% to 95.1%, a drop of just 2.5 percentage points.

states.label: When looking at percentiles
states.body: p95 is the value indicating that 95% of requests complete within a certain time when requests are ordered by speed. For example, with 100 requests, p50 is 2 seconds and p95 is 40 seconds, revealing the slow tail of requests. Therefore, delay SLOs are expressed as the requirement that a specified proportion of requests (e.g., 95% or 99%) respond within a defined time. LLMs tend to have longer response times as output length increases, making the tail of the delay distribution prone to elongation. Hence, instead of using the average, higher percentiles should be used as SLIs to avoid missing the slowness experienced by a small subset of users. Quality should also be analyzed both overall and by customer segment to reveal potential declines among specific customer groups.

screens.outro: Having determined how to handle delay and quality, let's now see what to classify as an incident.

screens.title: Definition of Incident
screens.lead: While reading the examples in the table, consider where NIST Glossary definitions apply to each example.

data.caption: Case in light of incident definition
rows: An external user sends input exposing internal documents to the model, and the documents actually appear in the response.
This is an event that actually compromised the confidentiality of information.
Although no data leak has occurred, it was discovered that an access key has been uploaded to a public repository.
Even without an actual breach, a potentially compromising threat can become an incident.
An employee violated the acceptable use policy and pasted customer information into a chatbot on a personal account.
Violations of our security policy and acceptable use policy are also included in the definition.
Due to planned maintenance, service was briefly stopped at an expected time.
The change was planned and approved and did not jeopardize or violate policy.
data.notes: In the NIST glossary, an incident is an event that actually or potentially jeopardizes the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of an information system or information, and includes a violation or imminent threat of a security policy, procedure, or acceptable use policy. Because operational failures and security incidents may overlap, they are classified within the same response framework and severity criteria are documented in advance. Cases that are difficult to distinguish based on definition alone, such as the last row, are examples where judgment may vary depending on the organization's classification criteria.

screens.outro: When an incident that falls under the definition occurs, you can respond by knowing what happened and in what order. What makes this possible is chronological recording.

screens.title: Audit Trail: A record that can be reconstructed in order
screens.lead: Read the history from top to bottom to restore the order in which a single request was processed. The record below is an example format to illustrate the concept.

data.code:
02:11:07 User u-1042 | Question entered | Request r-77
02:11:07 Service a-chat | Prompt v9 applied | Request r-77
02:11:08 Service a-chat | Model m-large called | Request r-77
02:11:10 Model m-large | Tool refund-api call request | Request r-77
02:11:10 Service a-chat | Tool call approval | Request r-77
02:11:11 Tool refund-api | Return response error | Request r-77
02:11:12 Service a-chat | Send response to user | Request r-77
02:40:00 Responsible party kim | Roll back prompt v9 to v8 | Change c-31

notes.note: Who did what, when, and what was left along with the request number to restore which prompt version and model the user's question led to. An audit trail is a chronological record that allows you to reconstruct the order in which a transaction or process occurred from start to finish.

In AI services, it records which tool the model attempted to call, whether the call was approved, and what results the tool returned. This is the basis for determining whether an error occurred in the tool or the model.
You should also leave the user informed of what actually went out. What happens under the hood and the results you receive may vary.

Response actions are also recorded in the same records. Although this is not a requirement in the NIST definition, practice ensures that records cannot be modified after the fact and that they are retained for as long as necessary. That way, you can trust and use the same records during the incident and in the subsequent cause analysis.

screens.outro: Even if records are in place, preparations are scattered if there is no established framework for how the organization will view the response. In the next screen, let's read the incident response guidance perspective.

screens.title: Incident Response Guidelines (NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3)
screens.lead: The text on this screen is NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 (confirmed in April 2025, CSF 2.0 Community Profile). Select sentences to see which aspect of the guidelines each contains.

data.text:
This procedure does not treat incident response as a separate process.  
It is recommended to integrate the response into cybersecurity risk management activities in general.  
This enables the organization to prepare for incidents.  
The number of incidents occurring and their impact can be reduced.  
It can also improve the efficiency and effectiveness of detection, response, and recovery activities.  
The implementation method is recommended to be read in conjunction with online materials for supplementary understanding.

marks.span: It is recommended to integrate the response into cybersecurity risk management activities in general.
marks.note: Rather than viewing response as a separate procedure that only takes place after an incident occurs, response is viewed as part of risk management as defined by CSF 2.0. This means that daily preparation and response during an incident become a cycle.

marks.span: This enables the organization to prepare for incidents.
marks.note: Preparation occurs before an incident. Establishing predefined contact methods, severity criteria, and record items falls under this category.

marks.span: The number of incidents occurring and their impact can be reduced.
marks.note: The effectiveness of the guidelines goes beyond handling incidents well and extends to reducing the number of incidents and damage. This is why the post-mortem improvement item goes back to contrast.

marks.span: It can also improve the efficiency and effectiveness of detection, response, and recovery activities.
marks.note: It refers to how quickly and effectively detection, response, and recovery are carried out when an incident occurs.

marks.span: The implementation method is recommended to be read in conjunction with online materials for supplementary understanding.
marks.note: The instruction document itself does not contain all possible implementation methods. Specific procedures tailored to an organization's environment must be established along with supplementary materials.

screens.title: Oncall: How notifications reach people
screens.lead: Review the typical structure from advancing to the next step until the alert reaches the responsible party.

steps.title: Notification goes to Teams
steps.body: On-call is a rotating responsibility system where individuals respond to alerts (pages). Sending alerts to a team responsible for a service is more stable than sending them directly to an individual, as alerts would be missed if that individual is on vacation.

steps.title: Routing and Urgency
steps.body: Routing rules define the urgency level of alerts, the responsible team, and escalation policies. The severity level of SLO threats established in the earlier stage serves as the basis for urgency determination here. Routing also handles filtering out low-urgency alerts that would otherwise wake people up during the night. A distinction between alerts that rapidly decrease in volume—immediately escalated—and those that decrease slowly—logged as tickets—is a representative urgency criterion in routing.

steps.title: The schedule now determines who is in charge.
steps.body: Determine who is currently responsible for each shift. Shift schedules must be pre-established to account for shift changes, leave, and substitute personnel. If schedules are empty or outdated, there will be no place to send alerts.

steps.title: Response status and escalation
steps.body: Notifications usually go through the following states: raised, acknowledged, and resolved. If no one checks in within the given time, it will be escalated to the next person or higher level person. Escalation notifications stop when the responder acknowledges and accepts the notification. Confirmation is a sign that responsibility has been handed over.

screens.outro: Once you have determined the path through which the notification will reach the person, you must also determine the order in which the person will move after it reaches the person. Next, we will look at the timeline of failure response.

screens.title: View response sequence along the incident timeline
screens.lead: Move the sliders to see how your first actions and what you look at change through the five stages of incident response.

visual.alt: A timeline of detection, classification, response, recovery and confirmation, followed by post-mortem back to preparedness.

stops.body: An alert goes off and Page reaches the person in charge. The goal of this step is for the person to become aware of the event. Your first action should be to mark the notification as acknowledged so others don't have to respond twice.

Severity is determined by the scope of impact and threat SLO. See what was impacted, how many people were affected, and whether external customers were exposed. Only after classification is completed will it be decided who should be called in more. The severity level is determined by the organization. As an example, level 1 affects a large number of external customers and the budget is quickly reduced and is called immediately, level 2 is limited to a select group of customers and is responded to within business hours, and level 3 affects only internal users and is handled as a ticket.
Official responders coordinate and take mitigation measures. Even before the cause is fully identified, steps can be taken to reduce the impact. All actions and times are recorded.
Metrics confirm whether service is back to target range. The proof of recovery is not the fact that action was taken, but the fact that the SLI is back inside the SLO.

Audit trails and response records help reconstruct the sequence of events and determine measures to prevent recurrence. Improvements return to the next provision, such as alert routing, severity criteria, and history items. Post-mortem analysis is not a place to cover individual mistakes, but to find contributing factors to the system. If the person in charge determines that the information is incomplete, ask why the system provided only that information and correct the system and procedures. Blaming causes people to hide problems. The criteria for which post-event analysis will be used (e.g., when a user-visible failure exceeds a certain threshold or when there is an on-call intervention such as a rollback) are set before the incident occurs.

screens.title: Explanation 1: Sequencing responses based on scope of impact and service goals
screens.lead: Open the judgment steps of the case one by one and check on what basis the response order is decided.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: We simultaneously received notifications of delayed responses in customer chat and errors in our internal summary tool. The representative must decide which of the two notifications to open first. If there are no criteria, the notification that arrives first will be opened.

steps.title: Check your service goals
steps.body: Check the SLO and degree of violation for each service. Customer chats are used by external customers, so we compare whether response delays are cutting short the target, while internal tools allow for room in the target. The severity of violations can be compared by how quickly the error budget is decreasing, or burn rate, so that different services can be compared on the same basis.

steps.title: Compare scope of influence
steps.body: Compare how many users are affected and whether your external customers are exposed. Even if the same error is visible to thousands of external customers, the urgency level is different if it is visible to a few internal users.

steps.title: Order and division
steps.body: The side that has the greatest impact and threatens SLO more will be responded to first, and the other side will be assigned a separate person in charge to respond in parallel. It is important to ensure that one person does not alternate between the two. The designated person in charge and the basis for the decision will be recorded.

steps.title: conclusion
steps.body: Impact and goals determine the order, not which notification comes first. Service goals must be written in writing so that everyone can make the same judgment and work in the same order even in the early morning without rushing.

screens.title: Explanation 2: Why the response to cost abnormality notifications and quality abnormality notifications is different
screens.lead: Toggle the toggle to compare how the two alerts differ in their nature, what they first see, what mitigation actions they take, and what they call.

states.label: more than cost
states.body: Users may not experience any symptoms. The service is responding normally, but costs have increased abnormally, making it a problem of waste rather than availability. The first check is to break down usage by model, app, and tag to find where the increase has occurred. Mitigations include setting usage limits, throttling traffic, and blocking abnormal calls. The people you call will have different names depending on the organization, but they are usually finance and platform people. However, if an abnormal call originates from an attack or policy violation, it may fall under the definition of an incident, so we consider that possibility as well.

states.label: more than quality
states.body: The service responds normally, but the answer is incorrect. Since users are clearly affected, this is treated as an SLO violation. The first check is the previous changes and evaluation results. Determine when the prompt, model, or settings changed and when the symptom began. Mitigation includes rolling back previous changes, isolating problem customers, and temporarily moving to human review. The person to call will have a different name depending on the organization, but is usually responsible for quality and product. In both cases, records are kept for post-mortem analysis, but the callers are different.

screens.title: Commentary 3: Postmortem with records
screens.lead: Select each record item and see what questions it answers.

items.prompt: History of changes (prompts, models, settings) immediately before the failure started.
items.answer: The audit trail finds what changes were made immediately before the outage began. As the candidates for change are narrowed down, so are the causal hypotheses. This question cannot be answered if the change has not been recorded.

items.prompt: Time sequence of changes and symptoms
items.answer: The change must precede the symptom to be the cause. If the symptoms begin before the change, another cause may need to be sought. This order can only be confirmed if the time remains accurate.

If you put the time when the alert was sounded, the time it was confirmed, and the time when mitigation measures were taken, you can see the section where the response was delayed. Targets for improvement are determined by determining whether the delay is due to a lack of notification or a delay in making a decision.

The results of your analysis should go back to preparing for the next incident, such as alert routing, severity criteria, and enrichment of log entries. If improvement items are left without a deadline with the person in charge, the same incident will repeat itself.

items.prompt: Principle of analysis: It's not who's at fault, it's what made it so
items.answer: Post hoc analysis assumes that the person involved made a good faith decision based on the information they had at the time. If the judgment is wrong, find out why the system made the wrong judgment, whether there was insufficient information in the notification, or there was no record entry, and correct the system and procedures. Pointing out an individual will result in less recording and reporting in subsequent incidents.

screens.title: Key takeaways
screens.lead: Summarizes the content covered in this class in one place.

paragraphs: SLO is a promise that ties user-perspective measurements (SLI) to business value and ties them to goals. Having a goal allows you to know whether what is happening is an obstacle, and the degree to which it threatens your goal determines the urgency of your response. In AI services, response quality can also be SLI.

An incident in the NIST glossary is an event that actually or potentially jeopardizes the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of an information system or information. This definition serves as a starting point for classification as it also includes imminent threats and violations of policies and acceptable use policies. An audit trail is a record that allows you to reconstruct events chronologically. In practice, trust is maintained by making records irreparable and keeping them for as long as necessary.

NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 views incident response as part of cybersecurity risk management, helping to prepare, reduce the number and impact of incidents, and improve the efficiency and effectiveness of detection, response, and recovery. Oncall is a system where notifications reach people through teams, schedules, and escalation.

Response flows in the following order: detection, classification, response, recovery and verification, and post-mortem analysis. Order is determined by scope of impact and service objectives, not by which notification arrives first. Cost anomalies and quality anomalies have different first checks, different mitigation actions, and different targets for invocation.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Failures are defined by service objectives rather than operational status, sequencing is defined by impact and objectives, and post-event analysis is done based on records at the time of the incident.

screens.outro: All of the information listed is things you can prepare for before a disability occurs. Please check whether the standards, contact routes, records, and response procedures are in writing.

screens.title: Reflecting on Concept Cards
screens.lead: Select a card, turn it over, and summarize the key concepts one more time.

cards.back: SLI is a measurement of service behavior from the user's perspective, and SLO is a reliability goal set by linking SLI to business value. In AI services, response quality can also be SLI.

An event that actually or potentially jeopardizes the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of an information system or information. Also includes imminent threats and violations of our security and acceptable use policies.

It is a chronological record that allows you to reconstruct the order in which security-related transactions or procedures occurred from start to finish. It must be left from the time of the incident, and in practice, it is preserved for as long as necessary to prevent subsequent tampering.

It is a shift system that receives notifications and takes responsibility for responding. Notifications go to teams, routing rules and schedules determine who is responsible, and if there is no response, they are escalated.

We recommend integrating incident response as part of cybersecurity risk management rather than a separate process. This helps to prepare, reduce the number and impact of outbreaks, and improve the efficiency and effectiveness of detection, response and recovery. It is easy to understand it as a cycle where the improvement items in the post-analysis return to the next preparation.

The order of response is determined not by which alert arrives first, but by the number of users affected, exposure to external customers, and the degree to which it threatens SLO. Divide responsibilities and record the evidence so that one person does not handle two cases alternately.

glossary.def: Reliability goals set by linking SLI to business value.
It is a shift system that receives notifications and takes responsibility for responding.
An incident that actually or potentially jeopardizes the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of information and systems or violates policy.
It is a chronological record that allows us to reconstruct the order in which events occurred.
This is the process of sending a notification to the next person in charge when there is no response within a set time.

Error budget is the amount of failures your SLO allows. Burn rate is the speed at which the budget is consumed as a multiple of the allowable speed. The faster the response, the more urgent the response.

misconceptions.myth: If the service is running, it is not a failure.
misconceptions.fact: Even if the answer is wrong or slow, it is a SLO violation and may result in an incident.

misconceptions.myth: Respond to notifications that come first.
misconceptions.fact: Order by scope of influence and degree of threat to objectives.

misconceptions.myth: Records can be organized after the fact.
misconceptions.fact: An audit trail must be left from the time of the incident to enable reconstruction.

misconceptions.myth: If the average delay is within the target, the SLO is maintained.
misconceptions.fact: The average masks a small number of very slow requests and a dip in quality for some groups of customers. Delay should be defined by percentile such as p95 or p99, and quality should be divided by customer group.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: SLO is a standard that determines the urgency of response.
Incident definition and audit trail are the basis for classification and reorganization.
NIST guidance views response as part of risk management.
Oncall sets the path for notifications to reach people.
If the error budget decreases quickly, it is called immediately; if it decreases slowly, it is ticketed, and delays are defined as percentiles rather than averages.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Think about whether our AI service has a documented SLO and who gets called when a failure occurs. Where does my business get stuck with SLO?

checks.q: At a 99.9% SLO (30-day period), the failure rate remains at 1%. At what point does the burn rate and error budget run out?
checks.explain: The allowable failure rate is 0.1% and the actual failure rate is 1%, so the burn rate is 10. The budget is designed to be used over 30 days, so if you spend it 10 times faster, it will run out in about 3 days. If the consumption is this fast, it becomes the target of an immediate call.

wrong.0: Burn rate 1 is when the failure rate is 0.1%, which is the tolerance.
wrong.2: It cannot be less than 1 because the failure rate is higher than the allowable value.
wrong.3: 1% is not 100 times the allowable value, but 10 times.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. The results will not be recorded, so feel free to choose.

checks.q: The average response time is within the target, but we keep getting complaints from some users that it is very slow. How to change delayed SLI?
options: Measure averages to the nearest decimal point with greater precision
Defined as a percentile, such as p95 or p99, that determines whether a certain percentage of requests complete within a set amount of time.
Set server CPU utilization as SLI
checks.explain: The average masks a small number of very slow requests. If defined by percentile, slow requests in the tail are reflected in SLI.

wrong.0: Even if the precision is increased, the average has the same tendency to cover the tail.
wrong.2: CPU utilization does not directly indicate the delay experienced by the user.
wrong.3: Except for slow requests, the cause of frustration disappears from the metrics.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. The results will not be recorded, so feel free to choose.

checks.q: After a failure, we try to reconstruct the order in which input went through which model and which tool was called. What are the most appropriate conditions for recording?
options: Only metric average values are stored for a long time.
Remains in chronological order and cannot be modified for as long as necessary
Only the latest state is overwritten and saved.
Only requests with errors are sampled and stored.
checks.explain: An audit trail can be used for reconstruction only when it records who did what and when. In practice, it is managed to prevent falsification and preserve it for the necessary period.

wrong.0: The average value cannot reconstruct the order of individual requests.
wrong.2: If you overwrite it, the past order will disappear.
wrong.3: If only part of the text is left, the context cannot be connected.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. The results will not be recorded, so feel free to choose.

checks.q: Put the flow of failure response in order
items: Detection: An alert goes off and Page reaches the person in charge
Classification: Determine severity by scope of impact and threat SLO
Response: Official responders coordinate and take mitigation actions
Recovery and Verification: Verify with indicators that the service is back to target scope
